Got a mortgage protection letter after closing? What to check

A letter about mortgage protection that arrives after closing may be an advertisement for life insurance, not a notice from your lender. Mortgage protection is optional. Here is how to check who sent the letter and decide what to do.

By Luay Sadqi, Licensed Agent (NPN 21370662) · November 2026

Not long after closing, a letter or reply card arrives. It says “mortgage protection” and may show your lender’s name. Here is how a sender can know about your loan, what the coverage is and how to check the letter before you answer.

The short version: A letter like this may be an advertisement for life insurance, not a notice from your lender. Mortgage protection is optional. Before you reply, find out who sent it and confirm that the agent and the insurance company are licensed in your state.

Why a letter can arrive after closing

A home purchase or refinance creates public records. Deeds and mortgages are recorded in local land records, and those records are generally open to the public.

Virginia is one example. State law there says deeds, deeds of trust and mortgages of real estate are recorded in the clerk of court’s deed book (Va. Code § 17.1-227). With some exceptions, records kept by circuit court clerks “shall be open to inspection in the office of the clerk by any person” (Va. Code § 17.1-208).

Because records like these are open, a company you have not dealt with can learn who your lender is. The Tennessee Attorney General’s office made the same point in 2022, in an alert about a different kind of mailing (home warranty letters). It said some mortgage information, such as the name of your lender and servicer, is public record and can be found online (Tennessee Attorney General, June 29, 2022).

So a letter that shows your lender’s name did not necessarily come from your lender.

Mortgage protection is optional

Mortgage protection is life insurance, and buying it is your choice. The National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) explains how this works for credit insurance, which is insurance sold with a loan. If the insurance is optional, a lender cannot deny you credit for not buying it. The one exception the NAIC names is private mortgage insurance, or PMI (NAIC, November 1, 2008).

PMI is not the same thing as mortgage protection. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) explains it. You might have to buy PMI if you take out a conventional loan and put down less than 20 percent of the purchase price. PMI protects the lender. In the CFPB’s words: “Mortgage insurance, no matter what kind, protects the lender – not you – in the event that you fall behind on your payments” (CFPB, reviewed August 28, 2026).

To see what your lender asked for, look at your own closing papers. The CFPB says lenders generally require proof of homeowner’s insurance. It also says a monthly PMI premium “is shown on your Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure on page 1, in the Projected Payments section” (CFPB, reviewed November 9, 2026).

What kind of coverage it is

Mortgage protection is life insurance. When it is a term life policy, two kinds matter, and a letter may not say which one it means. The NAIC describes them (NAIC, updated November 14, 2025):

  • Level term. The death benefit and the premium are fixed for the length of the term.
  • Decreasing term. The death benefit goes down over time. The NAIC says this kind is often used for debts that get smaller, such as a mortgage.

How to check who sent it

  1. Find the names. Look for the agent or agency and the insurance company. Virginia’s rules on life insurance advertising, for example, say “The name of the insurer shall be clearly identified in all advertisements about the insurer or its products” (14VAC5-41-90). Other states set their own rules. If the letter shows only a program name, ask which licensed agent sent it and which insurer would issue the policy.
  2. Look up the license. Not sure about a company? The NAIC’s advice is to contact your state insurance department. Confirm that the company or agent is legitimate and licensed in your state. The NAIC’s page for state insurance departments lets you choose your state and has an agent search. Our state pages name each regulator, such as Virginia, Maryland and Texas.
  3. Read how it presents itself. The same Virginia rule covers advertisements that look like material from a non-insurance company you already deal with, such as a lender. An advertisement may not do that in a way that leads you to believe “the purchase of insurance is required by the company.” If a letter leaves you unsure, your state insurance department takes questions and complaints.

A notice from your own lender or loan servicer is a different matter. The CFPB gives one example. If you do not have homeowner’s insurance, your lender is allowed to buy it for you and charge you for it, but must give you advance notice. If you cannot tell who sent a letter, ask your lender, using the contact details on your loan statement.

How to decide

An advertisement does not need an answer. If keeping the home in the family matters to you, take these steps in your own time.

  1. Count what you already have. Add up the life insurance you own, including any through work. Compare it with what you owe on the home and what your family would need. A letter is not a reason to drop coverage you own.
  2. Ask what kind of policy it is. Our mortgage protection page has a short list of questions to ask about any coverage offered with a loan, and a list of what to compare. They work for a letter too.
  3. Get a second quote. Ask for a quote on a level term policy for the same amount and the same number of years. Then put the two side by side.

Common questions

Mortgage protection letter FAQ

Is a mortgage protection letter from my lender?
It may not be. Some mortgage information, such as the name of your lender, is public record, so another company can print it on a mailing. Look for the sender's own name on the letter. If you want to be sure, ask your lender using the contact details on your loan statement.
How did they get my name and mortgage information?
Public land records are one possible source. Deeds and mortgages are recorded there, and the records are generally open to the public. In Virginia, for example, state law says records kept by circuit court clerks are open to inspection by any person, with some exceptions.
Do I have to respond to a mortgage protection letter?
Not if it is an advertisement. Mortgage protection is optional life insurance. The mortgage insurance a lender may require, called PMI, is a different product that protects the lender. If you cannot tell who sent a letter, ask your lender using the contact details on your loan statement.
Is a mortgage protection letter legitimate?
Mortgage protection is a real kind of coverage. It is life insurance meant to cover a home loan. Whether a particular sender is licensed is something you can check. Find the name of the agent and the insurance company on the letter, then confirm both with your state insurance department.
What kind of insurance is a mortgage protection letter offering?
Mortgage protection is life insurance. If it is term life, it may be level term, where the death benefit is fixed, or decreasing term, where the death benefit goes down over time. A letter may not say which kind it means, so ask before you compare it with anything else.
